title: Improving Judgments
coreMove: Change the process through which judgments are formed, not merely the awareness or intentions of the people forming them.
sourcePressure: Visible noise creates pressure for improvement. But improvement means changing the structure of the process — the order of information, who deliberates with whom, what a scale point means — not merely raising awareness or exhorting people to be more consistent. Awareness of noise does not reduce it. Process changes do.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Assuming that informing people about noise will reduce it, or that more experienced or more careful judges will automatically produce less noise without structural changes.

sourceAnchors.name: Process-level noise reduction approaches
sourceAnchors.detail: The book's recurring remedy theme is that noise reduction requires process design — sequencing information, structuring aggregation, anchoring scales — rather than character development or awareness training.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Telling people about noise makes them wince. It does not make them more consistent. Changing the process they use makes them more consistent whether they winced or not.

hook: you can improve your judgment starting today
the best decision-makers have one thing in common
counterintuition: effort and intention don't improve judgment
the worst way to fix judgment is to try harder
tryThisNow: resolve to slow down your next big decision
write a pre-mortem before your next important choice
examples: a scene where someone simply decides to try harder and immediately makes better decisions — that is awareness not process
a scene where the improvement is a personality change or mindset shift rather than a structural process change

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Improvement examples risk all reading as 'team decides to do things differently and things get better.' Different formats and entry points are needed to show the contrast between awareness-only approaches (which fail) and genuine process changes (which work).

exampleSpecs.domain: refugee status determination: a refugee agency comparing outcomes before and after a structured assessment protocol introduction
exampleSpecs.audience: a refugee agency regional director piloting a new case-decision protocol
exampleSpecs.stakes: consistent protection for people fleeing persecution — with outcomes previously varying by 35 percent across officers handling comparable cases
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: contrast the pre-protocol period (awareness training was given; officers were told to be consistent; variation remained at 35 percent) with the post-protocol period (intermediate assessments recorded before final decision; variation fell to 14 percent) — showing that the process change succeeded where the awareness campaign had not
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two lines on a trend chart: an officer-level variation metric over time, the line flat through the awareness-training period, then declining sharply at the point the protocol was introduced
mustInclude: the specific process change (intermediate recorded assessments)
mustAvoid: implying the awareness campaign was wasted or pointless — it might have helped acceptance of the protocol; it just did not reduce noise on its own

exampleSpecs.domain: customs and border screening: comparing officer-level inconsistency before and after restructuring the inspection checklist
exampleSpecs.audience: a border security training officer reviewing inconsistency data from two pilot stations
exampleSpecs.stakes: both security effectiveness and traveler fairness — inconsistent screening means some travelers are burdened more than others for identical profiles
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: two training officers compare the screening inconsistency data from the station that received only the awareness briefing versus the station that received the restructured checklist: the awareness station's variation is unchanged after six months; the checklist station's variation is down by 20 percent; the training officers discuss what that difference means for the next rollout
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a side-by-side comparison chart for two stations pinned to a training room corkboard — variation bars for the awareness-only station and the checklist station side by side for six months
mustInclude: the divergent outcomes (unchanged vs. 20 percent reduction)
the implication for process design over training alone
mustAvoid: implying either station's officers were less competent

exampleSpecs.domain: medical claims handling: an insurance company introducing independent assessment before supervisor review to reduce noise
exampleSpecs.audience: a claims quality director piloting a new sequencing rule for complex medical claims
exampleSpecs.stakes: consistent claim decisions and fraud detection — a noisier process produces both unfair denials and undetected fraud
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director presents the pilot results to the leadership team: under the old process (claims handlers discussed complex cases before recording their assessments) the inter-handler variability for matched claim types was 28 percent; under the new sequencing rule (individual assessment before group discussion) variability fell to 11 percent
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a quality dashboard on a conference room screen showing two variability bars — one for the old process, one for the new — the new bar clearly shorter
mustInclude: the specific process change (sequencing individual before group assessment)
the mechanism explanation — individual assessments before discussion prevent the first voice from anchoring everyone else
mustAvoid: attributing the old variability to individual handler carelessness

exampleSpecs.domain: radiology: a hospital requiring second opinions on borderline imaging findings and measuring the effect on overall read variability
exampleSpecs.audience: a radiology department chief who introduced a mandatory second-opinion protocol for borderline findings
exampleSpecs.stakes: diagnostic accuracy and patient safety — borderline findings are exactly where noise is highest and outcomes are most consequential
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: six months after the protocol introduction, the department chief reviews the data: for findings classified as borderline, the discordance rate between initial and second-opinion reads was 18 percent before the protocol and remains 15 percent after it — a smaller reduction than expected — because the second-opinion reader was being briefed on the initial finding before completing their independent read, meaning the independence was contaminated
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a discordance rate chart showing the period before and after protocol introduction, the line dropping slightly but not as much as projected, with an annotation at the expected drop point that says 'independence contaminated'
mustInclude: the protocol being partially effective because independence was not fully preserved
the contamination mechanism (second reader knew the first result)
the lesson: process improvement requires process precision, not just process intention
mustAvoid: framing the partial improvement as a failure

exampleSpecs.domain: geological survey interpretation: a mining company standardizing the sampling protocol used by two independent survey teams
exampleSpecs.audience: a chief geologist trying to reduce the variation in ore-grade estimates between her two field teams
exampleSpecs.stakes: project investment decisions — ore-grade estimates that vary by 20 percent across teams make feasibility calculations unreliable
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you are reviewing the results of the protocol standardization: the sampling method is now identical across both teams, but the ore-grade estimates still vary by 12 percent, down from 20 percent but still above the investment decision threshold — meaning the process change improved but did not solve the problem, and the remaining noise lives in the interpretation step that was not standardized
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two geological maps of the same site drawn by two different field teams, their ore-grade contour lines showing different patterns despite using the same sampling points
mustInclude: the remaining 12 percent residing in the unaddressed interpretation step
your decision about what to standardize next
mustAvoid: implying either team used incorrect geology

exampleSpecs.domain: management performance appraisal: a consultancy firm introducing calibration sessions after initial individual manager ratings are recorded
exampleSpecs.audience: a human resources director building a new performance review cycle
exampleSpecs.stakes: fair compensation decisions and employee retention — appraisal noise creates pay disparities for equivalent performers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the HR director asks: if managers submitted their ratings before rather than after seeing each other's ratings in the calibration session, would the calibration session produce genuine convergence on accurate ratings or would it simply produce conformity to the first visible ratings? The answer from the pilot is: in 60 percent of calibration conversations, the second manager to speak adjusted their rating toward the first — regardless of who was more accurate
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a calibration session room where the ratings have just been revealed on a shared screen — the second and third managers looking at the first manager's ratings before they have fully committed to their own
mustInclude: the distinction between genuine convergence and social conformity in calibration
the implication: individual ratings before any comparison, then calibration on divergences only
mustAvoid: implying any manager intentionally inflated or deflated ratings

skillTargets: explain why awareness of noise is insufficient to reduce it
identify which specific process change in a described scenario would reduce noise versus which change would only increase awareness
apply process-change thinking to design a noise-reduction intervention for a given judgment system
analyze why partial process improvements (like the contaminated second-opinion case) still leave residual noise
evaluate whether a proposed intervention targets noise at the process level or only at the awareness level

tryThisNowSpec: Think of one judgment process you run — a hiring panel, a grant review, a weekly rating decision. Write down one specific process rule you could introduce before the next cycle: not an attitude to adopt, but a structural step that would constrain when information is shared or when ratings are recorded. That is the unit of improvement this chapter is about.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one short paragraph (2-3 sentences) making the awareness-vs.-process distinction crisply, at least one 5+ sentence paragraph showing why good intentions in a noisy process produce noisy outcomes, at least one one-sentence punch line about what process change does that intention cannot
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one direct second-person passage asking the reader to name one process rule in their domain that was designed to reduce noise and whether they actually measured whether it worked
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
